title: Engineers saved the Leaning Tower of Pisa by removing soil
body: Pisa’s bell tower began to lean during construction in the 12th century because its foundations sat on soft clay and sand. By 1990 it tilted about 5.5 degrees and was closed over fears it could topple. Rather than push it upright, engineers slowly drew out small amounts of soil from beneath the high side, letting the tower settle back. By 2001 it had straightened by about 45 centimetres, enough to keep it stable for an estimated 200 years.

slides.heading: A lucky pause
slides.text: Building stopped for almost a century during wars, giving the soil under the first storeys time to compact. Without that pause, it would likely have toppled.

slides.heading: A tower that bends
slides.text: Later builders tried to compensate by making upper floors taller on the lower side. As a result, the tower is actually slightly curved.

slides.heading: Fixes that backfired
slides.text: Earlier attempts to stabilise it, such as injecting grout into the foundations in the 1930s, actually made the lean worse.
